title: Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services

reading.body:
Scammers created AI-generated videos using the real face and identity of a named South Florida immigration attorney to run fraudulent social media accounts offering fake legal services to immigrants. The operation ran across TikTok, Facebook, and Instagram, directing victims to WhatsApp where they were sent fake contracts and charged roughly $2,200 per transaction. The failure here is impersonation: AI tools were used to fabricate convincing likenesses of a real person, deployed outside any legitimate service context and with no human check on the other end except the fraudsters themselves.

The scheme was not caught by the platforms but by the attorney's own office, which noticed it only when defrauded clients began calling. Removal of nearly 6,500 fake profiles required a hired anti-piracy firm, not platform-side detection. That gap between creation and removal shows the platforms had no automated or human review capable of catching coordinated synthetic-media impersonation at scale before harm reached victims.

Whether any specific individuals or organizations behind the scam have been identified, charged, or prosecuted is not established by the reporting.

reports.title: Scammers steal identity of renowned Miami attorney to target immigrants on social media
South Florida immigration attorney says AI scammers are using his identity to target immigrants
Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services
Legal resident loses thousands seeking citizenship to AI immigration attorney

summary:
Angel Leal, a South Florida immigration attorney with over 30 years of experience, has become the target of artificial intelligence scammers who are using fake videos and social media profiles with his likeness to defraud vulnerable immigrants. The criminals have created hundreds of fraudulent accounts offering immigration services that Leal never provides, often requesting $2,200 payments for fake residency assistance. Leal discovered the scheme when potential clients began calling his office last October, though the situation has dramatically worsened in recent months. His firm hired an anti-piracy company that has successfully removed nearly 6,500 fake profiles across social media platforms, including 3,500 from TikTok, 2,400 from Facebook, and 544 from Instagram.

The scam typically begins with AI-generated videos directing viewers to contact a WhatsApp number, where fraudsters exchange emails and send fake contracts to victims. Leal warns immigrants to be cautious of anyone requesting payments through apps like Venmo, Zelle, or Cash App, and to verify the identity of legal service providers online. He has changed his personal phone number due to the fraud and plans to contact local and federal authorities this week to investigate the origin of the scams and launch a formal investigation.
